Annals of Family Medicine

The List

Schiefer R · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Reflective essay / narrative commentary (not original research; no methods or data reported).
Key Question: How can humanistic, person-centred care be taught and modelled to family medicine residents amid the time pressures of inpatient rounds?
Key Findings:
  • No quantitative or formal qualitative findings are reported; the abstract describes three clinical encounters used as narrative illustration.
  • The author identifies a recurring tension between task completion ("the list") and connecting with patients as people.
  • The essay suggests residents' own emotional and human needs are as easily overlooked as patients', though this is not empirically tested.
Clinical Relevance: Highlights the hidden curriculum and workload pressures affecting trainee wellbeing and compassionate care, which resonates with GP trainers and educational supervisors in the NHS working under sustained time and workload constraints.
Limitations: Not applicable in the conventional sense for a reflective piece, though the observations derive from a single author's perspective in a US inpatient setting and are not generalisable evidence.

Annals of Family Medicine

Prescriber Practices and Barriers to Providing Prescription Medication Instructions for Patients With a Non-English Language Preference

Manzor B, Ramírez JL, Lanchoney OWL et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Cross-sectional survey (questionnaire) of outpatient prescribers at a single US academic health centre.
Key Question: What are prescribers' practices and barriers in providing non-English prescription instructions to patients with a non-English language preference?
Key Findings:
  • 169/477 (35.4%) prescribers responded; 61.5% were unaware of best practices for providing non-English medication instructions to patients or pharmacies.
  • 91.8% did not tell patients they could request a non-English label from the pharmacy.
  • 69.8% lacked confidence that these patients received accurate written medication instructions.
Clinical Relevance: Although US-based, the findings highlight a likely parallel risk in UK primary care, where language barriers may compromise prescribing safety and where interpreter use and pharmacy communication are inconsistent.
Limitations: Low response rate from a single academic centre, with self-reported practice and a predominantly White physician sample, limits generalisability and risks non-response bias.

Annals of Family Medicine

What It Cost and What It Gave to Become an Undocumented Family Physician

Ruiz J · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Reflective personal essay (opinion/narrative); not original research.
Key Question: How does being an undocumented immigrant during US medical training shape a family physician's practice and understanding of patients facing structural exclusion?
Key Findings:
  • The author describes repeated institutional barriers during training, driven by perceptions of undocumented trainees as a risk rather than any lack of ability. DACA allowed progression but did not remove uncertainty.
  • The author, now in rural family medicine with obstetrics, identifies parallels between their own experience and patients who delay or avoid care because of fear, mistrust, or exclusion.
  • The central argument is that systems conflate legality with worth, at a cost to communities.
Clinical Relevance: Although set in the US immigration context, it offers a perspective relevant to UK practice, where undocumented migrants and others facing charging or data-sharing concerns may delay or avoid primary care, and it may inform inclusive workforce and patient-engagement thinking.
Limitations: Not applicable (single-author reflective essay; no empirical data, so findings are experiential and not generalisable).

Annals of Family Medicine

Quality Improvement in Residency: Training, Projects, and Outcomes

Harriett LE, Wright KM, Anderson L et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Cross-sectional national survey of US family medicine residency programme directors (CERA 2025).
Key Question: How are quality improvement (QI) curricula delivered in US family medicine residencies, and which training and project features are associated with graduate QI proficiency?
Key Findings:
  • Response rate 44.2% (321/726). Most programmes used hybrid (46.8%) or locally developed (38.8%) curricula; core faculty provided most oversight (54.2%).
  • Graduate QI proficiency was rated mostly intermediate (63.5%); resident data access was limited in 44.6% and full in only 27.6%.
  • Higher proficiency was significantly associated (all P < .05) with hybrid curricula, fewer data-access barriers, project continuity, and greater dissemination/implementation of outcomes. Effect sizes not reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Findings suggest the value of longitudinal, well-supported QI training with data access, relevant to UK GP training programmes and supervisors designing QIPs for the RCGP curriculum and ARCP.
Limitations: Proficiency was rated by programme directors (subjective, self-reported), with a sub-50% response rate and cross-sectional design precluding causal inference; US-based, so transferability to UK training is uncertain.

Annals of Family Medicine

Identifying Hazardous Alcohol Use in Primary Care: Concordance Between Phosphatidylethanol and Self-Reports

Månsson V, Hammarberg A, Guterstam J et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Retrospective cohort study (Swedish regional primary care records linked to national registries).
Key Question: How well do phosphatidylethanol (PEth) levels agree with self-reported measures (AUDIT score, weekly drinks) in identifying hazardous alcohol use in primary care?
Key Findings:
  • Prevalence of hazardous use varied by method: AUDIT ≥8 identified 26.5%, PEth >210 ng/mL 14.6–18.3%, and ≥10 drinks/week 8.5%. Each method identified patients missed by the others.
  • PEth correlated moderately with AUDIT and weekly drinks, but non-linearly.
  • At similar PEth levels, men and higher-education/income patients reported more weekly drinks, while younger patients scored higher on AUDIT.
Clinical Relevance: PEth is increasingly available in UK practice, but this suggests it should complement, not replace, structured questionnaires (e.g., AUDIT-C) and consumption history.
Limitations: Retrospective design using tests ordered at clinician discretion (likely selecting higher-risk patients), with no gold-standard comparator, limits generalisability to routine UK screening.

Annals of Family Medicine

Assessing 5-Year Outcomes of a Teamlet Care Model in Singapore Polyclinics: A Matched Difference-in-Difference Analysis

Wye Wong SK, Tan KB, Pang J et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Retrospective matched cohort study with difference-in-differences analysis (national administrative data, Singapore).
Key Question: Does a small-team ("teamlet") care model (2 family physicians, 1 nurse, 1 care coordinator) improve clinical outcomes, care processes, utilisation and costs over 5 years in patients with diabetes, hypertension or hyperlipidaemia?
Key Findings:
  • Clinical gains were modest: HbA1c fell 0.1% (only in a subgroup without prior rising HbA1c), systolic BP fell 0.65 mmHg, LDL fell 0.03 mmol/L.
  • Process measures improved versus controls: 16% more diabetic foot screening and 6% more eye screening.
  • Utilisation shifted to primary care: lower inpatient (SGD 2,432), specialist (SGD 130) and ED (SGD 49) costs per person, offset by higher polyclinic costs (SGD 479); net saving SGD 2,186 per patient.
Clinical Relevance: Supports continuity-focused, team-based chronic disease management, relevant to NHS general practice workforce models, though the clinical effect sizes are unlikely to be meaningful.
Limitations: Retrospective observational design risks residual confounding, and the Singapore polyclinic setting and cost structures limit transferability to UK general practice.

Annals of Family Medicine

AI-Enhanced Super-Resolution Handheld Ultrasound for Carotid Plaque Detection in Community Screening

Lan J, Liu S, Chen H et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Diagnostic accuracy/model development and validation study (Hyper-CycleGAN super-resolution model), with a community-based validation phase.
Key Question: Can AI-enhanced handheld ultrasound improve carotid plaque detection and stenosis grading in community screening, compared with standard handheld ultrasound?
Key Findings:
  • Plaque detection rose from 87.6% (standard HHUS) to 94.8% (AI-enhanced) in 117 community participants with 153 plaques.
  • Agreement with the reference standard for stenosis grading improved (weighted κ 0.492 to 0.836).
  • Sensitivity for ultrasound-defined vulnerable plaques increased from 47.4% to 63.2%, with specificity remaining high (figure not reported in abstract).
Clinical Relevance: Low-cost, portable carotid assessment could support stroke risk stratification in community settings, but this remains investigational and is not currently part of NHS practice or screening pathways.
Limitations: Small, single-population cohorts with a portable ultrasound reference standard (not CT/MR angiography or clinical outcomes), and sensitivity for vulnerable plaques remained modest at 63.2%.

Annals of Family Medicine

Integrating Peer Support Into Medicare-Funded Care: A Qualitative Study of System-Level Insights From Early Implementation

Ferrin AA, Khudaier SE, Martinez J et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Qualitative study (semi-structured interviews, n=20; rapid analysis guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research).
Key Question: What barriers and facilitators affect early adoption of Medicare's new principal illness navigation peer support (PIN-PS) reimbursement codes?
Key Findings:
  • Barriers: low awareness of the codes, administrative and billing complexity, patient cost-sharing, and limits on reimbursable service time.
  • Facilitators: perceived benefits for care coordination and workflow, alignment with wider policy priorities, and organisational readiness to embed peer support in care teams.
  • Views differed across clinical and organisational settings; no quantitative outcomes were reported.
Clinical Relevance: This is US-specific (Medicare), so it is not directly transferable, but it offers insight for UK practice on funding and embedding peer support, comparable to social prescribing link workers and PCN-funded roles, where reimbursement design and administrative burden influence uptake.
Limitations: Small sample (n=20) of mixed stakeholders from early implementation only, with no assessment of patient outcomes or effectiveness.
